I spent a lot of last year wondering if I was learning the right things at the wrong time. AI keeps getting better at writing code, so the question stopped being “How do I code faster?” and became “What skills still matter when coding itself gets cheaper?” That question followed me into Y Combinator Startup School in San Francisco last weekend Hearing Jensen Huang , Alexandr Wang , and Boris Cherny talk about the future of software made one thing feel obvious: the people who win in AI won’t just be the fastest coders. They’ll be the ones who understand systems, abstraction, and how to build things that hold up in the real world. I really liked how Jensen Huang pushed back on the idea that AI destroys jobs. His argument was that AI automates tasks, not jobs. Coding gets faster, radiology reads get automated, legal work gets easier. But that often creates room for people to take on more work that was previously impossible to get to. It’s not that work disappears. It’s that the range of work expands, and the people who adapt get to do more of the meaningful stuff. But the part that hit hardest was the room itself. Meeting builders from all over the world who are already shipping ambitious products made the future feel less abstract. It’s one thing to talk about AI changing software. It’s another to be standing in a room full of people already building the next version of it. As someone working on trust infrastructure for AI agents, I left with a clearer conclusion: the real bottleneck isn’t code generation. It’s trust, reliability, and judgment. Huge shoutout to all the cracked people I met this weekend, and to the YC founders and partners who made it unforgettable. ...more

For years, we've evaluated AI systems one interaction at a time: prompt in, response out. But agents change that. They accumulate context, preferences, and memories across conversations. That sounds powerful until you ask a simple question: What happens when one of those memories is wrong? This weekend at the UC Berkeley AI Hackathon hosted by Cal Hacks , my team built Immune to explore exactly that problem. Using Redis vector search for memory storage and retrieval, Anthropic for reasoning, Arize AI for tracing, and Sentry for poison alerts, we focused on helping agents identify which memories may have led them astray in the first place. Coming into the weekend, I had never really thought about improving agents themselves. Spending 24 hours thinking about memory, reliability, and trust made me realize how many fascinating problems still exist below the application layer. What surprised me most was how different the problem felt from traditional software. A bad output isn't always the model's fault: it might be making a perfectly reasonable decision based on a bad memory written days or weeks earlier. As agents become more personalized and autonomous, memory stops being just a feature and starts becoming infrastructure. Huge thanks to my teammates Vineeth Reddy Vallapureddy Oleksandr Voievodin and Siddhi Prajapati for an incredible weekend. Curious to see how the ecosystem tackles memory integrity as persistent agents become the norm. As agents become more personalized, who's making sure their memories stay trustworthy? Read more on our Devpost: https://lnkd.in/gHmHXQ63 #CalHacks #AgenticAI ...more ...more

Everyone's worried about AI hallucinating. I'm honestly more worried about it remembering the hallucination. AI assistants keep long-term memory now, little notes about you that carry across separate chats. It’s useful, but it means someone can quietly feed one a lie. Picture your assistant "learning" one false fact - that a scam site is safe, or that you approved a payment you never made. Problem is, your agent doesn't forget it. It just keeps making slightly worse calls for you, and you'd never know which memory broke it. We built Immune to address this. Immune works by elimination: it finds which memories caused a bad decision and removes them, leaving the smallest set that was actually responsible. Even a lie planted five times to survive a one-by-one check still gets caught. It never asks another AI who's to blame, it isolates the culprit by proof, then locks it away. Memory is what makes agents actually useful, and it's the part nobody's guarding. Built on Redis vector search, Anthropic Claude, traced with Arize AI , and poison alerts via Sentry Huge thanks to Vineeth Reddy Vallapureddy Saanvi Bhargava and Siddhi Prajapati for making it real and Cal Hacks for giving so many memories! #AIagents #AISecurity #CalHacks #buildinpublic ...more

Just got back from Y Combinator Startup School, and I’m still processing the weekend. Listening to Jensen Huang , Sam Altman, Garry Tan , and so many incredible founders in one place was surreal. Everyone shared wisdom and inspiration, such as how and why there has never been a better time to do a startup, and how getting through one day at a time, resilience, matters most. Sitting in a stadium with builders from over 120 countries, this rang true. I also loved learning about what everyone around me was building. Almost every conversation was about a different problem space. This weekend strengthened my inner voice; my resolve and motivation to build. Thank you Y Combinator for bringing us together.

I went to YC Startup School today and here's 5 things Jensen Huang touched on that resonated with me. His best answers were all really about how to solve difficult problems. 1. Problem solving and reasoning should be reconstructed from first principles. If you have strong systems thinking & abstract level thinking, there's infinite potential to solving difficult problems. This applies to DSA too imo (stop grinding patterns). 2. "How hard could it be" should be the mindset going into any difficult problem regardless of how hard it truly is. That's how you push through instead of getting scared away at the start. 3. Everyone should have their own pocket AI, and tools like OpenClaw & Hermes are amazing for that. Build agents specifically tailored for your needs. 4. Every era of growth came from abstracting away some kind of work. Steam abstracted muscle and software abstracted process, and the AI revolution abstracts away coding itself. Thinking & reasoning are now the most important skills. 5. AI will not reduce jobs, it will grow the backlog. When AI becomes 10x more capable and can do the tedious, repetitive work, engineers get greedier & more ambitious about which problems are worth solving. The list gets longer, and they hire more people to work through it. We were never really limited by how much we could build. We were limited by how many problems we thought were worth attempting. What is on your list now that you thought was unrealistic just 1 year ago?

I met Boris Cherny , Head of Claude Code, at YC Startup School 2026! In the past quarters, Claude Code has become a core part of my workflow at the Structures-Computer Interaction Lab of UCLA , helping me move quickly from research ideas to real experiments. Boris’s emphasis on giving models room to play and be creative inspires me to think differently about how I can use AI as a collaborator in research. I’m excited to experiment with my new Claude credits and dive even further into how these tools can accelerate robotics. As part of my robotics research, I remember reading Physical Intelligence 's VLA papers to better understand techniques for robot learning. It was surreal to hear Chelsea Finn speak in person about the future of physical AI, driven forward by her work in compositional generalization, training robots to adapt to completely new scenarios. Beyond learning from these speakers, I’m grateful to have met fellow ambitious builders. It was wonderful sharing ideas and hearing different perspectives that motivate people to create. Thank you, Y Combinator , for such an inspiring Startup School experience!

YC SUS just ended! Last weekend I went to YC Startup School and did what everyone does — filmed clips, photographed slides, took messy notes. I then fed all of it to my AI twin on bestmate The result is live at https://lnkd.in/en9iS9nU - a knowledge graph of what eight speakers (Jensen Huang, Sam Altman, Patrick Collison, Alexandr Wang, Boris Cherny, and more) actually said. Every claim is cited and labeled by fidelity — verbatim, repaired transcript, or paraphrase because I didn't want machine-transcription errors in real people's mouths. Every session is askable, and answers come only from what was said on stage. My phone videos play right on the graph as receipts. The part I'm most excited about: it's collaborative. If you were there, you can add your own notes and takes and the graph shows where the room's judgment converges, the same way it maps where the speakers converged without coordinating.
